title: Lightning and thunderstorms: what to do
asks: what to do in a lightning storm
caught in a thunderstorm where is safe
is a car safe in lightning
is it safe to shelter in a shed during lightning
thunder is getting close what do i do
lightning while swimming or in a boat
can i use running water during a thunderstorm
someone got struck by lightning what do i do
litening storm wat do i do
thunderstorm rolling in fast, where do we go, over
answer: When thunder roars, go indoors. When you hear thunder or see lightning, immediately get inside a sturdy building or an enclosed vehicle with a metal roof.

Caught outdoors with no sturdy building or metal-roofed vehicle within reach: this library has no guidance for that situation. All of its advice on where to shelter from lightning is FEMA's, on this card, and it is about getting to a sturdy building or an enclosed vehicle with a metal roof.
Do not take shelter in small sheds, gazebos, dugouts, bleachers or a convertible car.
If necessary, take shelter in a car with a metal top and sides. Do not touch anything metal.
If boating or swimming, get to land and find a sturdy, grounded shelter or vehicle immediately.
When you expect thunderstorms, plan to be near sturdy shelter. Find a safe location nearby that you can go to immediately at the first sound of thunder.
During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and landline phones: electricity can travel through plumbing and phone lines.
Unplug all chargers when the storm arrives.
Watch for fallen power lines and trees.
warnings: Lightning can cause temporary unconsciousness, difficulties in breathing, or difficulties with the heart (irregular heartbeat).

Someone struck by lightning: pay close attention to the airway and breathing, check for other injuries, treat for shock and get medical aid (Army first aid manual, burn care). If the person is not breathing, start rescue breathing immediately; if the heart has stopped, CPR. The steps are on this library's CPR card.

quotes.text: When thunder roars, go indoors. When you hear thunder or see lightning, immediately get inside a sturdy building or enclosed vehicle with a metal roof.
Do not take shelter in small sheds, gazebos, dugouts, bleachers, or in a convertible car. If necessary, take shelter in a car with a metal top and sides. Do not touch anything metal.
If boating or swimming, get to land and find a sturdy, grounded shelter or vehicle immediately.
When you expect thunderstorms, plan to be near sturdy shelter. Find a safe location nearby to immediately go to at the first sound of thunder.

Charge your mobile phone before the storm arrives. Unplug all chargers when the storm arrives. During thunderstorms, avoid running water or using landline phones. Electricity can travel through plumbing and phone lines. During thunderstorms, pay attention to alerts from public officials. Watch for fallen power lines and trees.
High voltage electrical burns from an electrical source or lightning may cause temporary unconsciousness, difficulties in breathing, or difficulties with the heart (irregular heartbeat).
All burn care consists of— • Monitoring the casualty for life-threatening conditions. • Checking for additional injuries. • Treating for shock (if applicable). • Seeking medical aid.
Close attention to the casualty’s airway, breathing is required and always assess for secondary injuries and shock.
If the casualty is not breathing, immediately start rescuing breathing and seek medical aid.
CPR is conducted using a specific technique to provide manual circulation support during cardiac arrest or when the heart has stopped beating effectively.

conflict: No disagreement between sources. Dependency for the owner: the second warning points to the CPR card (cpr-adult); approve this card only together with that one, or remove the pointer sentence. Gap, now stated on the card: the kit has nothing for a person caught in the open with no building or vehicle (searched every document for 'lightning' and 'thunder': only FEMA P-2064's Thunderstorm, Lightning, and Hail section, ATP 4-02.11 para 12-10, and unrelated hits). The second warning is built from ATP 4-02.11's burn chapter (paras 12-10, 12-13, 12-14), where lightning is named with high voltage electrical burns, and from its rescue-breathing and CPR text; no kit document has first aid written specifically for a lightning strike. The first sentence of ATP 4-02.11's warning box ('Do not touch the casualty or the electrical source with your bare hands') is left out because it refers to a live electrical source, as the reviewer confirmed.
